paras: The lynching of Lunn Whittaker was the hanging of a Black prisoner by twenty to thirty masked, armed men who took him from the county jail at Quincy, Gadsden County, Florida, early on Sunday, April 17, 1881. Whittaker, described as one of the men implicated in the murder of James McJunkin, was hanged from an oak in the woods just east of town while the jail guards were made to watch. Wire briefs carried the story to papers in several states through late April, often garbling his name and the place.

In March 1881 a Bainbridge, Georgia, dispatch reported that "the negro who murdered James McJunkin near Quincy" had been captured twelve miles above Bainbridge by a party of ten Black men, had confessed, and had been taken to Tallahassee. The dispatch, which noted a four-hundred-dollar reward, did not name him. According to the Weekly Floridian of Tallahassee, the trial of "the persons charged" with McJunkin's murder caused a great deal of excitement in Quincy in the week before the lynching. On the Friday morning set for the trial, a prisoner the paper called "the negro Williams" was found to have broken out of jail and escaped.

Between two and three o'clock on Sunday morning, the Quincy Herald reported, twenty or thirty armed men "clad in blouses and well masked" entered the county jail. The guard, three or four young men who were singing to pass the time, were surrounded and held under cocked navy revolvers. The men took Whittaker from the room where he was confined and forced the guards to come with them.

About a quarter of a mile from the jail, in the woods just east of town, they hanged him from a limb of a black oak with an ordinary plow-line. The Herald wrote that the noose was badly adjusted, that his suffering "must have been horrible," and that he "fought desperately" while the guards looked on. Word spread through town that morning, and a large number of people went to view the body.
The Herald named none of the men, calling them only "the Vigilantes," and no report of an inquest, arrests, or other official action appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News carried the first report, a Quincy dispatch of April 17, under the headline "A Florida Lynching," and the next day reprinted the Herald extra as a "Graphic Description of the Hanging of Lunn Whittaker." The Weekly Floridian ran the same text on April 19 under "Lynch Law in Gadsden," preceded by its note on the trial week and the escape. The Herald's account mixed close detail with jokes, saying the guards were "most unceremoniously 'bounced'" and that Whittaker was "probably in a warmer region than Florida" because he was "pretty thoroughly known" to be "the prime cause" of McJunkin's assassination.

A Jacksonville dispatch of April 18 reduced the story to one sentence about a "colored man" charged with assassinating "a leading citizen" of the county, printed in Ohio, California, Missouri and Minnesota. A second wire, from Columbus, Georgia, on April 25, named the victim Louis or Lewis Whittaker and the murdered man "M. C. Jenkins (White)," and placed the lynching at "Gladsen" or "Gudysden," which some papers located in Georgia or Alabama. The Omaha Daily Bee ran an Atlanta version under "Lynch Law in Florida," while the Portland Daily Press headed the Columbus item "An Alleged Colored Murderer Lynched." These papers added no comment, and several printed the item in crime columns beside the lynching of a Black woman in Laurens County, South Carolina.

Reports disagree on the time: the Herald gave two to three o'clock Sunday morning, the Delaware State Journal "Saturday morning," the Columbus wire "Saturday night," and the Atlanta dispatch "about four in the evening." The Quincy dispatch and the Herald, written on the spot, are the better evidence for the early hours of April 17. The victim appears as Lem. Whitaker, Lunn Whittaker, and Louis or Lewis Whittaker, and the murdered man as James McJunkin or M. C. Jenkins. The Herald counted three or four guards, the Atlanta dispatch nine.

accounts.label: Jacksonville wire

accounts.label: Columbus and Atlanta wires
accounts.gist: Louis or Lewis Whittaker, charged with murdering a white man named M. C. Jenkins or McJenkins, was taken from jail by masked men or thirty horsemen and hanged to an oak, on Saturday night or 'about four in the evening'.

framing.detail: The Quincy Herald, reprinted under 'Graphic Description of the Hanging of Lunn Whittaker', joked that the guards were 'bounced' and that the victim was 'in a warmer region than Florida' since he was 'pretty thoroughly known' to be guilty.
The Weekly Floridian headed the Herald text 'Lynch Law in Gadsden' and added the trial-week context without comment.

Northern and western papers ran one-sentence briefs ('A Florida Lynching', 'An Alleged Colored Murderer Lynched', 'Lynched.', 'Lynch Law in Florida') in crime columns, often beside the Laurens County, S.C., lynching of a Black woman.

versions.value: Between 2 and 3 a.m. Sunday, April 17 ('last night' in an April 17 dispatch)

conflicts.note: The Quincy dispatch and the local Herald extra, written on the spot, are the better evidence for the early hours of Sunday, April 17.
The local Herald gives Lunn; the Columbus and Atlanta wires a week later give Louis or Lewis.
The Florida and Savannah papers consistently say McJunkin; the Georgia wires appear to garble the name.
Distant briefs turned the county name into a town and sometimes moved it to another state.
The local Herald is the closer source.
The March 1881 capture report suggests the murder was recent.
